parts.visual:
You launched your product. The 'Tech Nerds' love it. You have 10,000 passionate users. But when you try to sell it to regular, everyday people, they refuse to buy it. You are stuck.

The Technology Adoption Life Cycle:
1. The Early Adopters: Visionaries who will buy broken, new technology just because it is cool.
2. The Early Majority: Pragmatists who only buy a product when it is completely safe, proven, and used by their peers.
3. The Chasm: The massive, lethal gap between these two groups. Most startups fall into the chasm and die.
parts.audio: Crossing the Chasm is the most difficult transition in a startup's life. You must stop marketing to visionaries and figure out how to sell a safe, boring, and complete solution to the pragmatic early majority.

questions.question: A founder pitches a Fortune 500 CEO. The founder says: 'Our software is revolutionary, untested, and completely disrupts the industry!' The CEO passes. Why?
options: The CEO is the 'Early Majority' (a pragmatist). They don't want a revolution. They want a safe, reliable tool that reduces risk and has a 24/7 customer support line. The founder pitched to the wrong psychology.
questions.correct_answer: The CEO is the 'Early Majority' (a pragmatist). They don't want a revolution. They want a safe, reliable tool that reduces risk and has a 24/7 customer support line. The founder pitched to the wrong psychology.
questions.explanation: What excites an early adopter terrifies the early majority.

questions.question: Listen to the marketing director. How do you successfully cross the chasm?
questions.tts_text: We cannot attack the whole market at once. We must pick a tiny, highly specific niche. We become the absolute #1 dominant product for that one specific niche. Once we conquer the beachhead, we expand.
options: The 'Bowling Pin' Strategy. Pick a very narrow niche (the lead pin) and dominate it so completely that you become the safe, default choice. Then, knock over the adjacent niches.
questions.correct_answer: The 'Bowling Pin' Strategy. Pick a very narrow niche (the lead pin) and dominate it so completely that you become the safe, default choice. Then, knock over the adjacent niches.
questions.explanation: Facebook crossed the chasm by focusing exclusively on Harvard students before expanding.

questions.question: Why is 'Social Proof' the ultimate weapon for crossing the Chasm?
options: The Early Majority will not buy a product unless they see another pragmatic person in their industry using it successfully. They require peer validation to mitigate their perceived risk.
questions.correct_answer: The Early Majority will not buy a product unless they see another pragmatic person in their industry using it successfully. They require peer validation to mitigate their perceived risk.
questions.explanation: Case studies and testimonials are the bridge over the chasm.

questions.question: What is the 'Whole Product' concept in Geoffrey Moore's framework?
options: Early Adopters will buy an incomplete product and fix it themselves. The Early Majority demands the 'Whole Product': the software, the training, the customer support, and the integrations. Everything must work perfectly out of the box.
questions.correct_answer: Early Adopters will buy an incomplete product and fix it themselves. The Early Majority demands the 'Whole Product': the software, the training, the customer support, and the integrations. Everything must work perfectly out of the box.
questions.explanation: Crossing the chasm requires shifting from an engineering focus to a customer success focus.

pairs.match: Visionary customers willing to take risks on new, unproven technology
Pragmatic customers who buy only when a product is proven and safe
The difficult transition between selling to early adopters and the early majority
Focusing all resources on dominating one highly specific niche market first
